title: Uranus Is at Its Best and Brightest Tonight
summary:
One of the hardest planets to see in the solar system is putting on its best show of the year. On Wednesday, November 25, the distant ice giant Uranus reaches its annual opposition, its closest point to Earth this year, and will appear at its brightest.

Opposition happens when Earth passes between Uranus and the sun, so the planet sits "opposite" the sun in our sky. The moment of opposition falls at 6 p.m. ET on November 25. Uranus will rise in the east around sunset, reach its highest point around midnight, and set in the west around sunrise.

You can find it in the constellation Taurus, close to the Pleiades open star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters. Uranus will be a few degrees southeast of the cluster, about two-fifths of the distance between the Pleiades and Aldebaran, the brightest star in Taurus.

At magnitude +5.6, Uranus is technically visible to the naked eye under very dark skies. But binoculars or a good backyard telescope will make it much easier to find, and through a telescope it appears as a tiny blue-green disk. Its colour comes from methane in its atmosphere, which absorbs red wavelengths of sunlight. At opposition, Uranus is 18.4 astronomical units from Earth, about 1.7 billion miles away.

Named after Ouranos, the ancient Greek god of the sky, Uranus is one of the least understood planets in the solar system. A day there lasts about 17 hours, and the planet rotates sideways. It takes 84 Earth years to orbit the sun. Uranus also has 13 faint rings and at least 29 known moons, the most recent found in 2025 by the James Webb Space Telescope and named Uranus XXVIII. Many of its moons are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.

The distant planet has been visited only once, by NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft on January 24, 1986. Scientists now think the planet gives off its own internal heat, which could increase pressure on NASA to prepare a Uranus Orbiter and Probe, a mission concept the National Academy of Sciences recommended in 2022 as a high-priority planetary science mission. Uranus will stay well placed for a few weeks on either side of opposition, and will next come to opposition on November 30, 2027.
why_it_matters: Uranus is the hardest planet to see, so this is a rare chance to find it in the night sky. Learning about distant planets also helps scientists understand how our solar system works.

background_read: Planets travel around the sun, and the ones farthest away look faint and move slowly in our sky.
Sometimes Earth passes directly between the sun and another planet, which makes that planet easier to see.
Telescopes and binoculars collect more light than our eyes, so they help us spot faint objects in space.
Uranus is called an ice giant because it is made mostly of icy materials and gases, unlike rocky planets such as Earth.
